core: What promotion is: the working definition — any marketing communication used to inform target audiences of the relative merits of a good, service, brand, or issue, most of the time persuasive in nature (attributed to the AMA Universal Marketing Dictionary); stated plainly as the marketing activities that communicate an offering's value and persuade customers to act
Promotion as the fourth P of the marketing mix and the most visible part of marketing
The promotion mix and its five families: advertising, public relations, sales promotion, personal selling, and digital marketing — one line and one original example each
The communication idea: every promotion is a message sent through a channel to an audience, with noise and feedback in between
The three classic goals of promotion — inform, persuade, remind — with an original example of each
Integrated marketing communications: all the pieces should tell one story, illustrated with an original multi-channel example
The honest framing: promotion supports the other Ps and cannot rescue an offering that fails on product, price, or place; the marketing mix is only as strong as its weakest element
supporting: OpenStax Principles of Marketing and Introduction to Business list the promotion-mix elements with slightly different wording; this lesson names the five families the lists share
The communication process (sender, message, channel, receiver, noise, feedback) as the mechanism behind all promotion
Longer objective lists in the textbooks (awareness, trial, retention) treated as refinements of the inform-persuade-remind trio
outOfScope: Advertising practice and media decisions (sibling topic marketing:foundations:advertising)
Digital advertising mechanics — targeting platforms, auction models, measurement (sibling topic marketing:foundations:digital-advertising)
The marketing mix as a whole — product, price, place strategy (sibling topic marketing:foundations:marketing-mix)
What marketing is and the marketing concept (sibling topic marketing:foundations:what-marketing-is)

claims.claim: The working definition of promotion, from the AMA Universal Marketing Dictionary, is any marketing communication used to inform target audiences of the relative merits of a good, service, brand, or issue, most of the time persuasive in nature.

The promotion mix is the set of communication tools a marketer combines to reach customers, and its five families are advertising, public relations, sales promotion, personal selling, and digital marketing.
Promotion is an attempt by marketers to inform, persuade, or remind consumers and business buyers in order to influence their opinion or elicit a response.
All promotion works through a communication process: a sender encodes a message, transmits it through a channel to a receiver, and feedback and noise shape whether the intended meaning arrives.

Integrated marketing communications coordinates all promotional activities so the consumer receives the same message no matter which channel it arrives through; every piece of a campaign should tell one story.

A marketing communications strategy should be developed only after the rest of the marketing mix is set: the marketer defines the target market, builds the product, sets the price, and chooses distribution before deciding what to say.
Promotion supports the other Ps of the marketing mix but cannot rescue an offering that fails on product, price, or place; the marketing mix works only as well as its weakest element.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The promotion-mix element lists differ across authoritative sources: OpenStax Principles of Marketing 13.1 lists advertising, sales promotion, personal selling, public relations, direct marketing, and Internet/digital marketing, while OpenStax Introduction to Business 12.5 lists traditional advertising, personal selling, sales promotion, public relations, social media, and e-commerce.
positions: Principles of Marketing 13.1: advertising, sales promotion, personal selling, public relations, direct marketing, Internet/digital marketing
Introduction to Business 12.5: traditional advertising, personal selling, sales promotion, public relations, social media, e-commerce
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lists overlap on five families — advertising, public relations, sales promotion, personal selling, and digital — and the lesson names exactly those five, noting that the textbooks word the lists differently. This is a naming difference, not a substantive disagreement, and is stated in the lesson rather than hidden.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The working definition of promotion is worded differently across sources: the AMA Universal Marketing Dictionary emphasizes communicating the relative merits of a good, service, brand, or issue to target audiences, while OpenStax Introduction to Business 12.5 frames promotion as an attempt to inform, persuade, or remind consumers and business buyers to influence opinion or elicit a response.
positions: AMA dictionary: any marketing communication used to inform target audiences of the relative merits of a good, service, brand, or issue, most of the time persuasive in nature
OpenStax Introduction to Business 12.5: an attempt by marketers to inform, persuade, or remind consumers and business buyers to influence their opinion or elicit a response
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the AMA dictionary entry as the working definition, restates it in plainer words (communicating an offering's value and persuading customers to act), and attributes the inform-persuade-remind framing to OpenStax. Both formulations agree that promotion communicates and seeks a response, so the synthesis is faithful.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Some textbooks list more promotion goals than the classic three: longer lists such as awareness, trial, and retention appear alongside inform, persuade, and remind.
positions: Longer goal lists: awareness, trial, retention (and similar refinements)
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson treats the longer lists as refinements of the same three goals and says so explicitly, keeping the classic inform-persuade-remind trio as the framework while acknowledging the longer lists exist.

unsupportedExistingClaims: No prior draft existed for this topic; the lesson was written directly from source-verified research, so there are no unsupported draft claims to replace.
correctionsNeeded: Wrote the lesson from the verified source set: the AMA Universal Marketing Dictionary 'Promotion' entry (read live 2026-08-22) for the working definition; OpenStax Principles of Marketing 13.1 (Wayback capture 2025-02-10) for the promotion mix; 13.2 (Wayback capture 2024-01-18) for the communication process; 13.3 (Wayback capture 2024-01-18) for integrated marketing communications; OpenStax Introduction to Business 12.5 (registry record reused) for the inform/persuade/remind framing and mix elements; OpenStax Introduction to Business 11.3 (registry record reused) and CFI 4 P's of Marketing (registry record reused, re-verified live) for promotion's place in the mix and the weakest-element framing.
Documented the element-list and definition-wording differences among sources in conflictingEvidence rather than hiding them.
Named advertising, public relations, marketing mix, what marketing is, and digital advertising as sibling topics (reference only) in scope and relatedTopics.
Wrote five original scenario questions with a balanced answer key (A:1, B:2, C:1, D:1) including recall, application, and analysis items.

All business names, taglines, and scenarios in the lesson are original and fictional (Meadow Bakery, Riverton Bicycle Co-op, Gable Street Roasters, the taco truck, Salt & Stone pizza truck, Brightspark Repairs).
